Check that code tested on a de-identified copy should run on the original

Source: R/anon_fidelity.R
anon_check_fidelity.Rd

Compares a de-identified copy with the original data, property by property, and reports what code written against the copy relies on that no longer holds. Run it where the original data is, before sharing the copy; the result holds counts, names and rule parameters only, so it can be shared with the copy (see anon_report()).

Usage

anon_check_fidelity(original, deidentified, key = "USUBJID", dm = "dm")

Arguments

original

A data frame or a named list of data frames: the data before de-identification.

deidentified

The same as original after de-identification: a data frame, a named list of data frames, or the step that made it (such as an anon_deidentify() result). With a step, its log and settings say what was changed on purpose; without one, intended changes can't be told from others and are reported as "warn".

key

Name of the subject identifier column.

dm

Name of the subject-level dataset whose keys every other dataset's keys must be found in, and whose RFSTDTC study days are counted from ("adsl" for ADaM data without dm).

Value

A tibble of class "anon_fidelity" with columns dataset, check, status ("pass", "fail", "warn" or "not applicable"), n_checked, n_failed and detail (counts only), and attributes complete (TRUE when nothing was left uncompared: no subjects that couldn't be paired or told apart, no dates of subjects with no known offset) and passed (TRUE when the result is complete and no check failed). It prints, and converts with as_anon_payload() and as_anon_json().

Details

Each check compares a property in the original with the same property in the copy. It fails only when the property held in the original and is broken in the copy. A property already broken in the original is "not applicable", with the original's count.

A check that compared nothing is "not applicable", with the reason.

Aligning rows. anon_subject_ids() sorts rows by the new key, so the copy's rows don't line up with the original's. Subjects are paired by their rows, coded from the columns no step logged (and of the same class), in every dataset with key, in turn: rows that match exactly; then, of the rest, subjects with as many rows in every dataset and more than half of them equal (rows sharing a code with more than 20 unpaired subjects don't count, which keeps this linear; subjects with no other match stay unpaired); then rows that match in the columns with no value more often in the copy than in the original (a column changed throughout is left out); then, among subjects alike in those columns, each subject's own dates (their formats and their distances from the subject's first date, which the per-subject offset keeps). A step's kept pseudonym map (keep_secrets = TRUE) is used instead when there is one, and keys that weren't pseudonymized pair directly. Within a subject, rows pair in order. Subjects alike in every column no step logged and in their date pattern give the same result for every check whichever way they pair, so when the copy holds as many of them as the original, they are compared as a class: each copy subject is paired, in a fixed order, with an original whose values explain the cells a step logged (blanked, generalized or derived where the step says so, and otherwise equal), and the checks run on them. With offset dates, each pair's offset must be one the dates step can give (a full matching of the class is required). If no pairing explains them all, the subjects left fail. A very large class can't be paired this way: one whose logged cells take more than 250,000 combinations of an original's and a copy's values, or of more than 300 subjects that a greedy pass on their dates can't pair; it is reported as not compared, and the result is incomplete. Run the steps with keep_secrets = TRUE to pair such subjects by the kept map. A class with a different number of subjects in the copy can't be paired: those subjects are counted (pseudonyms is "warn"), their rows are not compared one by one, and the result is incomplete. A copy subject whose dates match none of the originals alike in the other columns fails. Rows of datasets without key pair by position.

Checks (one row per dataset and check; "(all)" for checks across datasets):

  • datasets: the same dataset names.

  • columns: the same columns in the same order.

  • types: the same class and type for each column, and for the columns of nested data frames (packed columns, and data frames in list columns).

  • attributes: the same dataset and column labels, formats (format.sas, format.spss, format.stata, display_width), time zones (tzone), factor levels (their set and order) and value labels. Value labels and levels of the key, related IDs and dates may change; a column another step logged keeps the original's levels in their order, less those no longer used, plus the fold category. In a dataset where the log of anon_subject_ids() or anon_subject_dates() counts labels it rewrote, a changed label whose original holds a key, a related ID or a date is "warn"; any other change fails, and so does a label lost.

  • rows: the same number of rows, or fewer only by the rows of subjects the step dropped ("warn", with counts). Rows of subjects that couldn't be paired are counted, and make the result incomplete.

  • row order: within each subject, rows in the same order.

  • keys in dm: every key of the dataset is in dm.

  • distinct keys: the original's number of subjects, less those dropped.

  • pseudonyms: each subject has one pseudonym in every dataset, and each pseudonym one subject: every copy subject's rows across datasets match one original subject's. Related IDs follow the pseudonyms, row by row: a column the IDs step replaces (SUBJID) holds the pseudonym's number, and a key column (RSUBJID) the pseudonym of the subject the original names, or a blank where it names a subject the data doesn't hold; a blank where the original named one fails.

  • values: every column no step logged keeps its values, row by row over the paired rows; the key, related IDs and dates have checks of their own. A cell a step logged may differ only by the change it logged: blank where a blanking step logged it; the band or rounding of the original value, or the fold's category where the rule folds the original's category (from the rule's parameters in the settings); numbers rewritten from a generalized result at the row's own conversion and decimals; recomputed values (the numeric relations check them); or a derived value that the original data pairs with the released value of its quasi-identifier. No more cells are blanked or changed than the log counts, test by test. A column logged for one test only is compared on the other rows. Copies of a column a step changed (AGE in adsl and in advs) must agree within each subject where they did in the original (dataset "(all)"). Packed data frame columns are compared the same way; data frames in list columns by their number of rows, and by their values when their rows keep their order (no key column, or one subject); the detail names each by its path (NEST[[]]$T).

  • categorical values: each value of a character or factor column is a value of the original column, a blank, or a value a step introduced on purpose (a fold category of a generalization rule, numbers rewritten from a generalized result). Key, related ID and date columns are checked by the other checks.

  • ISO 8601: each non-blank value of a *DTC column, or of a column a profile's "date" rule names, has the format and precision of the original value in its row. Values removed on purpose (not ISO 8601 in the original, partial dates with partial = "remove", rows without a key, columns a step blanked) are counted apart.

  • date intervals: within each subject, every date (text, Date and date-time columns, in every dataset) moves by the subject's offset, so the interval between any two is kept; clock times are kept. The offset lies within the dates step's range (min_days to max_days), or is 0 when a step ran that doesn't offset dates. Year-and- month dates are compared at month precision (the month of the original's day 15 moved by the offset, as anon_subject_dates() shifts them), and year-only dates must all move by one number of years, the subject's year step (max(1, round(|offset| / 365.25)), 0 for no offset).

  • study days: --DY recomputed from --DTC and RFSTDTC (SDTM rule, no day 0), and ADaM *DY from *DT and TRTSDT, agree with the copy's values wherever they agreed in the original.

  • numeric relations: CHG = AVAL - BASE, PCHG = 100 * CHG / BASE and --STRESN equal to the number in --STRESC, wherever they held in the original. Rows where a step changed one of the values on purpose (and logged it) are counted apart; if the relation no longer holds in some of them, the check is "warn".

Not checked: business rules beyond these; changes among subjects alike in every unchanged column and their date pattern that another pairing of them explains (they are compared as a class, and without the pseudonym map which one is which can't be known); the derived values of several quasi-identifiers beyond being blank or unchanged; values of data frames nested in list columns whose rows hold several subjects (their order changes), and dates and keys inside nested data; statistics (means and counts by group change with banding and suppression). A pass is evidence that code relying on these properties should behave the same on the original, not proof that it will.

Sharing the result. It names datasets and columns as the copy does, and never an original's name; print(), as_anon_payload() and as_anon_json() don't apply your pattern_list. To share it redacted, include it in a report: anon_report(step, fidelity = result, pattern_list = ...).

Cost. A few passes over every column of every dataset, plus groupings of the rows, linear in the number of rows: a few seconds for the pharmaversesdtm and pharmaverseadam datasets.

See also

anon_deidentify(), anon_report()

Examples

dm <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = sprintf("S%02d", 1:12),
  AGE = c(31, 34, 38, 42, 45, 47, 52, 55, 58, 61, 66, 69),
  SEX = rep(c("F", "M"), 6),
  RFSTDTC = format(as.Date("2020-01-01") + 0:11)
)
result <- anon_deidentify(list(dm = dm), max_risk = 1/3, seed = 1)
anon_check_fidelity(list(dm = dm), result)
#> Fidelity of the de-identified copy: passed 
#> pass: 12, warn: 0, fail: 0, not applicable: 0 
#> 
#>  dataset check              status n_checked n_failed
#>  (all)   datasets           pass    1        0       
#>  (all)   pseudonyms         pass   12        0       
#>  dm      columns            pass    4        0       
#>  dm      types              pass    4        0       
#>  dm      attributes         pass    4        0       
#>  dm      rows               pass   12        0       
#>  dm      row order          pass   12        0       
#>  dm      distinct keys      pass   12        0       
#>  dm      values             pass   24        0       
#>  dm      categorical values pass   12        0       
#>  dm      ISO 8601           pass   12        0       
#>  dm      date intervals     pass   12        0       
#>  detail                                                                                                                                                 
#>  1 dataset(s)                                                                                                                                           
#>  12 of 12 subject(s) paired by the rows of the columns no step changed; 12 of them alike in every unchanged column and in their dates, paired as a class
#>  4 column(s), in the same order                                                                                                                         
#>  4 column(s) with the same class and type, nested data frames included                                                                                  
#>  4 column(s)                                                                                                                                            
#>  12 row(s) in the original, 12 in the copy                                                                                                              
#>  12 paired subject(s); 0 with rows in another order                                                                                                     
#>  12 subject(s) in the original, 12 in the copy, 0 dropped                                                                                               
#>  24 value(s) of paired rows compared; 6 blanked on purpose; 6 generalized or derived on purpose                                                         
#>  12 non-blank value(s) in 1 column(s)                                                                                                                   
#>  12 non-blank value(s) in 1 column(s) of paired rows
